Archite
är´kīt
n. (a man of the Archi, a clan on the border of Ephraim)
From Archi, a place on the border of the Josephite territory near Bethel. It identifies one man in Scripture — Hushai, the friend of David, whose counsel saved a fleeing king.

Biblical Definition

Hushai appears at the lowest point of David's life, as the king climbs the Mount of Olives weeping: “And it came to pass, that when David was come to the top of the mount, where he worshipped God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent, and earth upon his head” (2 Samuel 15:32). David sends him back into the city to defeat the counsel of Ahithophel, and he goes: “And it came to pass, when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, was come unto Absalom, that Hushai said unto Absalom, God save the king, God save the king” (2 Samuel 16:16). The title David's friend is given by the narrator at the moment Hushai appears to change sides. Absalom, having heard Ahithophel advise an immediate pursuit, hesitates: “Then said Absalom, Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he saith” (2 Samuel 17:5). Hushai counsels delay, Absalom takes it, and the narrator states who was actually governing the decision: “For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom” (2 Samuel 17:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Archi as a place on the borders of Ephraim, and an Archite as an inhabitant of it.

ARCHI, n. A place on the confines of the tribe of Ephraim, near Bethel.

ARCHITE, n. A native or inhabitant of Archi.

COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct.

FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; in courts, an officer of confidence attached to the king.

STRATAGEM, n. An artifice, particularly in war; a plan or scheme for deceiving an enemy.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 15:32 — "And it came to pass, that when David was come to the top of the mount, where he worshipped God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent, and earth upon his head:"

2 Samuel 16:16 — "And it came to pass, when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, was come unto Absalom, that Hushai said unto Absalom, God save the king, God save the king."

2 Samuel 17:5 — "Then said Absalom, Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he saith."

2 Samuel 17:14 — "And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel. For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom."

Modern Corruption

The episode is read either as Scripture endorsing deceit or as a difficulty to be explained away, and the narrator's own explanation — that the LORD had appointed to defeat Ahithophel's counsel — is left unused.

expand to see more

Hushai's mission raises a real question, and it should not be dodged: he entered Absalom's court professing loyalty he did not hold. Some treat this as proof that Scripture approves deception when the cause is good; others strain to show that every word he spoke was technically true. The narrative itself neither commends nor condemns his method. It reports what he did, and then reports the cause of the outcome in words that belong to no human actor: the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. The chapter is not offered as an ethics case study. It is offered as an account of providence.

That is the point most worth recovering. Ahithophel's advice was, the text says plainly, good counsel — militarily correct, and it would have killed David that night. It failed not because Hushai out-argued him but because God had appointed that it fail. Ahithophel understood exactly what had happened, went home, set his house in order, and hanged himself. The Reformed doctrine of concurrence is written across this chapter: real men gave real counsel and made free decisions, and the outcome was determined before the first word was spoken.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Arki (H757), an Archite; rea (H7453), friend, companion; etsah (H6098), counsel; parar (H6565), to break or defeat.

expand to see more

Hebrew Arki (H757) — an Archite, of the clan of Archi near Bethel.

Hebrew rea ha-melek (H7453) — the king's friend, an office of confidence at court.

Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice; the counsel of Ahithophel and of Hushai.

Hebrew parar (H6565) — to break, frustrate, defeat; the LORD appointed to defeat it.

Hebrew tov (H2896) — good; the narrator's own word for Ahithophel's advice.

Usage

"“Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent” — on the Mount of Olives."

"“Hushai the Archite, David's friend” — the title given as he enters Absalom's court."

"“The LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel” — the real cause."
